messages.content:
Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: In women with Hashimoto's disease, depressive symptoms decreased with implementing dietary recommendations including consuming vitamin D-rich products.
Sentence: "Depression symptoms decreased with the implementation of some dietary recommendations, including the consumption of products rich in iodine, iron, zinc, selenium, vitamin D, vitamin A and polyunsaturated omega-3 fatty acids."
Measured as: depression symptoms (Beck Depression Scale)
Population: 219 women aged 20-50 with Hashimoto's disease
Intervention: Dietary behaviour of consuming vitamin D-rich products (self-reported, questionnaire)
Comparator: Less adherence to the dietary recommendation
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: 219
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: Vitamin D status was not significantly associated with depressive symptoms in female nurses.
Sentence: "Vitamin D status was not significantly associated with EDS, anxiety symptoms, or depressive symptoms, whereas EDS was associated with both anxiety and depressive symptoms."
Measured as: depressive symptoms (HADS)
Population: Female nurses working at a university hospital, mean age 32.4 years
Intervention: Serum 25(OH)D level (measured, not administered)
Comparator: Higher vs lower vitamin D status
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: not reported
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml

content.text: {"rationale":"Both are cross-sectional associations, but Study A's exposure is a self-reported diet pattern of many nutrients in Hashimoto's patients versus Study B's measured serum 25(OH)D in nurses, so the results diverge mainly through who was studied.","verdict":"genuine","reason":"population","also_differs":["intervention","outcome_measure"],"detail":"women with Hashimoto's disease (dietary vitamin D-rich foods, Beck scale) vs female nurses (serum 25(OH)D, HADS)"}
